title: Why Dogs Really Eat Grass (and 9 Other Animal Secrets)

intro.say: A polar bear's skin is pitch black. And its fur? Not a single hair of it is actually white.
An animal that risks its life every week just to poop. A cat whose voice box purrs all by itself.
Here are ten animal secrets, counted down. And number one is something your own dog probably did this week, and almost everyone gets the reason wrong. Stay for it.

scenes.say: Cows look like they just stand around chewing. But inside the herd, they are picking favorites, and science has measured it.
Cows choose preferred partners in the herd, and spend much of their time close to them. Two cows, side by side, again and again.
At the University of Northampton, a researcher studied dairy cows. She penned each one either with its best friend, or with a cow it barely knew.
Then she checked their heart rate and stress. With a best friend, the cows were calmer. With a stranger, more agitated. The strongest bonds formed young, at seven to eleven months.
And all that calm chewing? Cows have one stomach with four compartments, and they chew their cud for hours every single day.
Honeybees don't sleep through winter. They spend it shivering, every single day, until spring.
They pack into a tight ball called a cluster, and vibrate their flight muscles to make heat. The wings stay perfectly still.
A single bee on its own can die of cold at about twenty eight degrees Fahrenheit. But the center of the cluster stays around ninety five degrees, right where the queen sits.
Outer bees pack tight like a living blanket, and take turns crawling inside to warm up. Winter bees live four to six months. Summer bees? Just a few weeks.
Their fuel is honey saved all summer. And just one pound of it takes visits to about two million flowers. But the next animal shares warmth in an even stranger way.
In the Antarctic winter, it gets colder than minus fifty degrees, with brutal winds. And that is exactly when emperor penguins raise their chicks.
The father does the hard part. He balances the egg on his feet for about two months, and eats nothing at all the whole time.
To survive, they squeeze into giant huddles. Up to twenty one penguins can pack into a single square meter. Inside, the air can warm up to thirty five degrees Celsius.
But the birds on the edge are freezing. So every thirty to sixty seconds, the whole huddle shuffles a tiny step, five to ten centimeters, like a slow stadium wave.
Slowly, the frozen outsiders work their way into the warm center. Nobody stays cold forever. Everyone takes turns.

chapters.title: Camel humps aren't full of water

scenes.say: Almost everyone thinks a camel's hump is a water tank. It isn't. It is mostly fat.
One hump can store up to eighty pounds of fat. When food runs out, the camel lives off it, and the hump goes limp and flops over, like a deflated balloon.
So where is the water? A very thirsty camel can drink thirty gallons in about thirteen minutes. That would kill most animals.
Camels have oval red blood cells, which keep flowing even when the body is dried out. They can lose about a quarter of their body weight in water and survive.
And for sandstorms, they have two rows of eyelashes and nostrils they can close. The next animal has a sense that sounds almost like science fiction.

chapters.title: Why foxes dive head-first into snow

scenes.say: A fox stands in a snowy field, freezes, tilts its head, and suddenly leaps high into the air, diving head-first into the snow.
It is hunting a mouse it can't even see, hidden under the snow. The fox listens for tiny rustling footsteps, then pounces, mouth first.
In the Czech Republic, scientists recorded almost six hundred of these jumps by eighty four red foxes. And they found something nobody expected.
Foxes jumping toward the north-east caught their prey seventy three percent of the time. In most other directions? Just eighteen percent.
One idea is that foxes use Earth's magnetic field like a rangefinder. No wonder the red fox has spread wider across the planet than any other wild carnivore.

chapters.title: Why sloths climb down just to poop

scenes.say: Three-toed sloths live high in the treetops. Yet about once a week, they crawl all the way down to the ground, just to poop.
Down there, they are slow, exposed and easy prey. And the trip burns precious energy for an animal that barely has any to spare.
And when they finally go, it is a big one. A single bathroom trip can make up to thirty percent of a sloth's body weight.
In two thousand fourteen, scientists in Costa Rica found a clue. Tiny moths live in sloth fur. They lay eggs in the poop, and the young fly back up to a sloth.
Those moths help feed green algae in the fur, and the sloth eats that algae. It is still a theory. But the next animal's secret is hiding right on its head.
Elephants flap their ears all day long. It looks lazy. But those ears are giant radiators.
An African elephant's ear can be six point six feet long and four feet wide. And it is thin, packed with thousands of tiny blood vessels.
Elephants barely sweat, and they can't pant like a dog. So they pump warm blood into those ears. Flapping pushes air across, and cooler blood flows back into the body.
At any moment, about twenty percent of their blood is passing through the ears. Asian elephants live in shady forests, so their ears are much smaller.
They have one more trick. Elephants spray themselves with mud and dust, which works like sunscreen and keeps biting insects away.
The polar bear is the largest meat eater on land, and it is hiding a secret under its coat. Its skin is completely black.
And the fur? Not a single drop of white pigment. Each hair is see-through, with a hollow core in the middle.
That hollow core scatters sunlight, so the fur only looks white, exactly like snow does. Snow is made of clear ice, too.
Under the skin, a layer of fat up to four inches thick traps the heat. Their coat is so warm, adult males can overheat when they run.
Even their paws are built for ice, up to twelve inches across, like snowshoes. But the next animal has a sound that scientists argued about for years.
How does a cat actually purr? For years, scientists believed the brain had to fire off a signal for every single buzz.
Then, in two thousand twenty three, researchers in Vienna tested cat voice boxes in the lab. They blew only warm, moist air through them.
All eight buzzed at purring speed. No brain signal needed. The voice box did it all by itself.
The secret may be soft, fatty pads in a cat's vocal folds. They make the folds heavier, so they shake slowly, about twenty five times a second, like a deep, creaky human voice.
And it's not just house cats. Cheetahs purr too. Lions and tigers roar instead. Now, for number one, a habit almost every dog owner has seen.
Your dog is out in the yard, happily chewing grass. Most people think that means it feels sick. Usually, it doesn't.
Researchers in California surveyed over fifteen hundred dog owners. Sixty eight percent saw their dog eat plants daily or weekly.
But only eight percent of those dogs often seemed ill beforehand. And just twenty two percent regularly threw up afterward.
Young dogs graze even more often, and look sick even less. And wild wolves eat plants too, so it is an old habit from their ancestors.
One theory says plant fiber helps flush worms out of the gut. So a grazing dog isn't crying for help. It's just being a dog.

outro.say: So, which one surprised you the most? The black polar bear, the purring voice box, or the grass-eating dog? Tell me in the comments.
And if you want more animal secrets explained, subscribe. There is a new one every few days.
